To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the genetic heterogeneity of HNSCC tumors is a significant predictor of survival and that this heterogeneity is associated with a higher frequency of TP53 mutations and a higher frequency of mutations in the PIK3CA and HRAS genes.
the intra-tumor genetic diversity of head and neck cancer, measured by the number of mutations per tumor cell, is associated with shorter overall survival.

the intra-tumor genetic diversity of head and neck cancer tumors is associated with worse survival, and that a measure of this diversity can be obtained from tumor biopsies, which could be useful for clinical care.

the clinical implications of intra-tumor heterogeneity and its detection and measurement in head and neck cancers.
the clinical relevance of intra-tumor heterogeneity.
intra-tumor genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity in HNSCC, and its clinical implications, including the potential for its detection in biopsy specimens and its relation to treatment outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
intra-tumor genetic diversity is a feature of HNSCC that is likely to influence clinical outcomes and that should be considered in future clinical trials.
the presence of intra-tumor heterogeneity has been documented to have a significant negative effect on the survival of head and neck cancer patients.
intra-tumor genetic and epigenetic heterogeneity is a feature of many tumors that is associated with worse prognosis and is likely to be a factor in treatment failure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intra-tumor genetic diversity of head and neck cancer is high, and is related to poor clinical outcome.
intra-tumor heterogeneity, as assessed by the method we describe, has been shown to be a significant prognostic factor in HNSCC, but the clinical significance of this finding is not yet known.

the presence of intra-tumor heterogeneity within HNSCC tumors is a marker of poor prognosis, that it is associated with the presence of a more aggressive cancer cell phenotype, that it is a marker of the presence of more aggressive cancer cell subclones, that it is related to the presence of cancer cells with more extensive DNA damage, and that it is associated, at least in some cases, with the presence of cancer cell populations that are resistant to therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of high heterogeneity in a tumor is a marker for a more aggressive disease.
intra-tumor genetic differences among cancer cells are a significant problem in cancer treatment, and the problem is particularly severe in head and neck tumors.
intra-tumor genetic variation in HNSCC can be readily measured in a clinical setting using a relatively small biopsy specimen, and that this variation can be associated with poor clinical outcomes.
